# MEMORANDUM

**To:** [Supervising Attorney]
**From:** [Associate]
**Date:** November 11, 2026
**Re:** Givand Battery Recovery, LLC / Goulound Lithium Reclamation, Inc.: Buyer-side issues list for the APA, Disclosure Schedule and Escrow Agreement

---

## Bottom Line

The APA was signed September 22, 2026. The deal is $48,500,000 with a $4,850,000 indemnity escrow (APA §§2.5, 2.6). Five provisions leave Givand materially exposed:

* Two of them go to the core of what Givand thought it was buying: the Pellancourt offtake contract and the refining line.
* Two of them undercut the indemnity package that was negotiated in the LOI and APA: the escrow as sole source of recovery, and the New York law and forum clause.
* One lets Seller walk away from its post-closing obligations: unrestricted assignment.

**How to fix them.** The APA is signed, so items in the APA and Disclosure Schedule need a written amendment under APA §11.6. The Escrow Agreement is still a form to be signed at Closing, so it can be fixed directly.

**Timing.** The outside date is December 31, 2026 (APA §8.1(b)). As of signing, no one had requested the Pellancourt consent (Schedule 3.9, Item 1). We need to move quickly.

---

## Summary Table (most significant first)

| # | Priority | Issue | Location | Fix (short form) | Client call? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **High** | Pellancourt consent is missing from Required Consents | Disclosure Schedule, Schedule 6.2(c); APA §§6.4, 7.2(d) | Add it as a Required Consent and a closing condition | **Yes** |
| 2 | **High** | "Business" definition excludes black-mass refining | APA §1.1 (definition of "Business"); flows into §§2.1, 2.2(f), 6.7 | Conform the definition to the LOI so it includes hydrometallurgical refining | **Yes** |
| 3 | **High** | Escrow made the "sole and exclusive source of recovery," which overrides the cap carve-outs | Escrow Agreement §4.6, read with APA §§9.5(b), 9.7, 11.10 | Delete §4.6, or make it expressly subject to APA §9.5(b) | **Yes** |
| 4 | **Medium-High** | Escrow Agreement selects New York law and Manhattan courts, against the APA's Delaware law and Chancery forum | Escrow Agreement §9 (Governing Law; Jurisdiction), read with APA §§11.7, 11.8, 11.10 | Conform to Delaware law and Chancery jurisdiction | No (but tell the client) |
| 5 | **Medium-High** | Seller may assign freely and is then released | APA §11.4 (Assignment) | Make it mutual, require Buyer consent, no release of Seller | Yes (credit support) |
| 6 | Medium | Related clean-up items | Various | See "Other Points" below | Some |

---

## Detailed Issues

### 1. Pellancourt Offtake Consent Omitted from Required Consents (HIGH)

**Where.** Disclosure Schedule, Schedule 6.2(c) (Required Consents). Related provisions are Schedule 3.9, Item 1, Schedule 3.3(b), and APA §§6.2(c), 6.4 and 7.2(d).

**What the documents say.**
* Schedule 3.9, Item 1 discloses that the Pellancourt Cathode Feedstock Supply Agreement (§16.2) requires Pellancourt's prior written consent to either:
  * a change of control of Seller; or
  * any transfer of all or substantially all assets of the recycling business.
* Without that consent, Pellancourt may terminate on 30 days' notice (§16.3).
* This transaction is exactly that kind of transfer (APA Recital B).
* Schedule 6.2(c) nonetheless states: "The only Required Consents are" the Facility landlord consent and the NDEP permit transfers.

**Why it matters to Givand.**
* Seller's efforts covenant (APA §6.4) covers only Required Consents.
* The closing condition (APA §7.2(d)) also covers only Required Consents.
* As drafted, Givand has no walk right if Pellancourt refuses. Its only choice would be to close and take the risk that Pellancourt terminates 30 days later.
* The Pellancourt contract is worth about $21,000,000 a year. Pellancourt is committed on a take-or-pay basis to at least 70% of the Facility's refined output through 2030.
* The LOI (§§3, 9(c)) calls this contract "a key reason for the Transaction." It says Givand's valuation assumes the contract continues, and it made the Pellancourt consent an express closing condition. The APA dropped that condition.
* Because the consent requirement was disclosed, Givand likely has no rep breach claim under §3.3 or §3.9 if the contract is terminated.

**Recommended fix.** Amend Schedule 6.2(c) (and, if needed, APA §7.2(d)) to add:

> "3. the prior written consent of Pellancourt Cathode Materials, Inc., under Section 16.2 of the Pellancourt Supply Agreement, to the assignment of the Pellancourt Supply Agreement to Buyer and the transactions contemplated by the Agreement, including an express waiver of any termination right under Section 16.3 arising from those transactions, in form and substance reasonably satisfactory to Buyer."

Also seek the following:
* An immediate covenant that Seller will request the consent within five Business Days.
* A requirement that Seller keep Buyer informed and let Buyer take part in discussions with Pellancourt.
* Removal of the §6.4 no-payment limit for this consent, or an agreed cost split.
* If the consent slips past December 31, 2026, an extension of the §8.1(b) outside date at Buyer's election.

**Fallback position.** If Seller resists making this a condition, ask for one of the following:
* a specific indemnity plus a purchase price reduction or holdback tied to Pellancourt terminating within a set period after Closing; or
* a separate special escrow for that risk.

**Client flag.** We need Givand's view on two things:
* whether it would close without Pellancourt's consent at all; and
* whether it wants to approach Pellancourt directly (with Seller's agreement) given the timing.

---

### 2. "Business" Definition Excludes Black-Mass Refining (HIGH)

**Where.** APA §1.1 (definition of "Business"), which flows into APA §2.1 (Purchased Assets), §2.2(f) (Excluded Assets) and §6.7 (Non-Competition).

**What the documents say.**
* APA §1.1 defines "Business" as collection, discharge and mechanical processing of spent batteries into black mass, "**excluding any refining of black mass**."
* The LOI §1 defines the Business to include "hydrometallurgical refining of black mass." LOI §2.1(a) specifically lists the refining line (leach reactors, solvent-extraction circuits, lithium carbonate crystallizer).
* Disclosure Schedule 2.1(a), Item 7 lists the hydrometallurgical refining line as "equipment of the Business."
* Several other items in the folder relate to refining:
  * the refining patent (Schedule 3.8, Item 2);
  * the Cordell tolling agreement and the Basin reagent agreement (Schedule 3.9, Items 4 and 5);
  * 16 refining employees (Schedule 3.14).

**Why it matters to Givand.**
* *Asset transfer.* APA §2.1 conveys only assets "used primarily in the Business." APA §2.2(f) excludes "any assets not used primarily in the Business." Seller can argue that the following are Excluded Assets:
  * the refining line itself (rated at 8,000 tonnes a year);
  * the wastewater pretreatment plant serving it;
  * U.S. Patent No. 11,684,219;
  * the refining know-how.
* *The schedule does not save Givand.* Under APA §11.10, the APA prevails over the Disclosure Schedule. Listing the line on Schedule 2.1(a) may not be enough.
* *Effect on the offtake contract.* Without refining, the Facility cannot make the lithium carbonate, cobalt sulfate and nickel sulfate that Pellancourt buys. Issue 1 and Issue 2 together threaten the core economics of the deal.
* *Non-compete.* APA §6.7 restricts only "the Business." Seller would be free to refine black mass, which is the highest-value activity, anywhere in North America after Closing. The LOI §7 also covered "any business competitive with" the Business. The APA dropped that language.
* *Sufficiency rep.* APA §3.6 is measured against the narrowed Business, so it does not protect Givand here.

**Recommended fix.** Amend the definition:

> "'Business' means the business of collection, discharge, shredding and mechanical processing of spent lithium-ion batteries into black mass and the hydrometallurgical refining of black mass (including the production of lithium carbonate, cobalt sulfate, nickel sulfate and other refined products), as conducted by Seller at the Facility as of the date of this Agreement."

Also add the following:
* In §2.1(a): "including, for the avoidance of doubt, all items listed on Schedule 2.1(a), each of which is a Purchased Asset regardless of the extent of its use in the Business."
* In §2.1(f): an express reference to U.S. Patent No. 11,684,219.
* In §6.7(a)(i): extend the restriction to "the Business or any business competitive with the Business," consistent with LOI §7.

**Client flag.** Confirm the business team understands that the signed APA arguably does not convey the refining line. This should be a non-negotiable correction. If Seller pushes back, it suggests Seller intends to keep or monetize refining.

---

### 3. Escrow as Sole and Exclusive Source of Recovery (HIGH)

**Where.** Escrow Agreement §4.6 (Exclusive Source of Recovery), read with APA §§9.5(b), 9.7 and 11.10.

**What the documents say.**
* The APA cap is 10% of the Purchase Price (§9.5(a)).
* Under §9.5(b), the cap and basket do not apply to:
  * Fraud;
  * breaches of Fundamental Representations; and
  * Excluded Liabilities, including Pre-Closing Environmental Liabilities.
* APA §9.7 provides for recovery first from the Escrow Fund and "thereafter directly by Seller."
* Escrow Agreement §4.6 says the Escrow Fund is Buyer's "**sole and exclusive source of recovery** for all Losses … under Article IX …, including Losses arising from Excluded Liabilities." The only exception is Fraud.
* Under APA §11.10, the APA generally prevails, but **the Escrow Agreement controls on matters concerning the Escrow Fund**. Seller will argue §4.6 is exactly such a matter.

**Why it matters to Givand.**
* Seller can argue that all recovery is capped at the $4,850,000 escrow. That would cover:
  * breaches of Fundamental Representations, including title (§3.5);
  * all Excluded Liabilities, such as pre-Closing taxes, employee liabilities, debt and litigation; and
  * legacy contamination at a hazardous waste treatment facility that handles lithium, cobalt, nickel and acids.
* The escrow is released 18 months after Closing (Escrow Agreement §3.1). The environmental reps survive six years (APA §9.1(b)). After release, §4.6 could leave Givand with **no recovery at all** for late-emerging environmental claims, apart from Fraud.
* This reverses the uncapped carve-outs agreed in LOI §6 and APA §9.5(b).

**Recommended fix.** Delete Escrow Agreement §4.6. If the Escrow Agent wants language on the point, replace it with:

> "4.6 No Limitation. Nothing in this Agreement limits the amount of Losses recoverable by the Buyer Indemnitees under the Purchase Agreement or the sources from which they may be recovered, including the right of the Buyer Indemnitees to recover directly from Seller under Section 9.7 of the Purchase Agreement. This Agreement is subject in all respects to Sections 9.5(b) and 9.7 of the Purchase Agreement."

**APA amendment.** Revise APA §11.10 so the Escrow Agreement controls only the Escrow Agent's mechanical duties: deposit, investment, claim and objection procedure, and disbursement. It should not control the scope of, limits on, or forum for indemnification.

**Client flag.** Ask the client to confirm whether it obtained or plans Phase II data on the Facility (see Other Points). The answer affects how hard we push on this item and whether Givand wants a separate environmental escrow or insurance.

---

### 4. Escrow Agreement Governing Law and Forum Conflict with the APA (MEDIUM-HIGH)

**Where.** Escrow Agreement §9 (Governing Law; Jurisdiction), specifically §§9.1 and 9.2, read with APA §§11.7, 11.8 and 11.10.

**What the documents say.**
* APA §11.7 selects Delaware law.
* APA §11.8 gives exclusive jurisdiction to the Court of Chancery of the State of Delaware.
* Escrow Agreement §9.1 selects "the laws of the State of New York."
* Escrow Agreement §9.2 gives exclusive jurisdiction to state and federal courts "located in the Borough of Manhattan" for "any dispute concerning the Escrow Fund, including whether a Claim Notice is valid or payable."
* Because APA §11.10 lets the Escrow Agreement control on Escrow Fund matters, the APA does not cure the conflict.

**Why it matters to Givand.**
* Any disputed Article IX claim against the escrow would go to New York under New York law. That is where the first $4,850,000 of every claim would be paid from (APA §9.7).
* Any excess over the escrow, and all claims after release, would go to Delaware Chancery under Delaware law.
* The result is two proceedings on the same facts, with risk of inconsistent rulings, a fight over forum and duplicated cost.
* Seller can use the split as leverage in settlement.
* "Final Order" (Escrow Agreement §1.1) means an order of a court "under Section 9." A Chancery judgment could therefore fail to qualify as a release trigger for the escrow.

**Recommended fix.** Conform Escrow Agreement §9 to the APA:

> "9.1 Governing Law. This Agreement and all claims arising out of or relating to it are governed by the Laws of the State of Delaware, without regard to conflict-of-laws principles that would require the application of the Laws of another jurisdiction.
> 9.2 Jurisdiction. Each Party irrevocably submits to the exclusive jurisdiction of the Court of Chancery of the State of Delaware (or, only if that court lacks subject-matter jurisdiction, the state or federal courts located in the State of Delaware) for any action arising out of or relating to this Agreement or the Escrow Fund, including whether a Claim Notice is valid or payable."

**Fallback position.** If the Escrow Agent insists on New York for its own rights and duties, split the clause:
* New York law may govern the Escrow Agent's rights, duties and indemnity only.
* All disputes between Buyer and Seller, including the validity and payability of Claim Notices, go exclusively to Delaware Chancery under Delaware law.
* The Escrow Agent agrees to disburse on a final Chancery order.

Also conform the "Final Order" definition to cover orders of the court specified in APA §11.8.

---

### 5. Seller May Assign Freely and Be Released (MEDIUM-HIGH)

**Where.** APA §11.4 (Assignment).

**What the APA says.**
* Buyer needs Seller's consent to assign.
* Seller may assign the Agreement, expressly including its Article IX indemnity, the §6.7 non-compete, the §6.8 transition services and the Transition Services Agreement, "**to any Person without the consent of Buyer**."
* Once the assignee assumes in writing, Seller is **released**.

**Why it matters to Givand.**
* After selling substantially all its operating assets, Seller can move its obligations to a shell with no assets, distribute the $48.5 million in proceeds, and leave Givand without a creditworthy indemnitor.
* This matters most after the escrow is released at 18 months. The environmental indemnity runs six years, and the Fundamental Representations run to the statute of limitations plus 60 days.
* Seller could also assign the non-compete and transition services to a **competitor** of Givand. A competitor would then be the one providing Givand's accounting, IT and regulatory reporting for nine months.
* The clause is one-sided and is not supported by the LOI.

**Recommended fix.** Replace the second and third sentences of §11.4 with mutual language:

> "Neither Party may assign this Agreement or any of its rights or obligations under it without the prior written consent of the other Party, except that Buyer may, without Seller's consent, (a) assign its rights to one or more Affiliates, (b) collaterally assign its rights to any lender, and (c) assign its rights to any acquirer of all or a substantial part of the Business. No assignment relieves the assigning Party of any of its obligations under this Agreement."

**Client flag.** Raise credit support for the period after the escrow is released, given that Seller's operating assets leave with the deal. Options include:
* a parent or shareholder guaranty;
* a covenant that Seller will not dissolve or distribute proceeds below a minimum net worth during the survival periods; or
* R&W and environmental insurance.

---

## Other Points

1. **Escrow claim window and post-release recovery.** Claim Notices may be delivered only "on or before the Release Date" (Escrow Agreement §4.1). This is acceptable only if §4.6 is deleted (Issue 3) and APA §9.7's direct recourse against Seller is preserved.

2. **Order of precedence clause.** Narrow APA §11.10, as described in Issue 3. Also consider whether the Disclosure Schedule should control for the asset list on Schedule 2.1(a), or simply fix the definition (Issue 2). Fixing the definition is the cleaner route.

3. **Environmental diligence.**
   * LOI §9(a) contemplated Phase II sampling as a condition. The APA has no diligence condition.
   * APA §6.3 requires Seller's consent for invasive sampling.
   * Schedule 3.11 lists only Phase I reports (2020 and a July 2026 update) and "no other exceptions."
   * **Client flag:** confirm whether Givand wants to do Phase II before Closing. If so, ask Seller to commit now that it will consent.

4. **Refining-related contracts.** Once Issue 2 is fixed, confirm that the Cordell tolling agreement and the Basin reagent agreement (Schedule 3.9, Items 4 and 5) are clearly Assigned Contracts. Also confirm that the Basin notice obligation (Schedule 3.3(d)) is satisfied at Closing.

5. **Wilmington office lease (Oakhurst Plaza Associates LLC).** This is Givand's own sales-office lease. It is unrelated to the Goulound acquisition and raises no issues for this deal. The hazardous materials restriction in §7.2 (no batteries or black mass on the Premises) is a reminder for Givand's operations team but needs no action in our comments.

---

## Items to Raise with the Client Before We Respond

1. **Pellancourt.** Would Givand close without the consent? Does it want direct contact with Pellancourt? Should we push for an extension of the December 31 outside date?
2. **Refining line and Business definition.** Confirm that this is a must-have correction and that the business team is aware of the current drafting.
3. **Indemnity recovery and environmental risk.** Confirm the Phase II plan and appetite for a special environmental escrow or insurance.
4. **Credit support.** Does Givand want a parent guaranty or a net-worth covenant from Seller after the escrow is released?
5. **Overall approach.** Present items 1–5 as a single package of conforming corrections, consistent with the agreed LOI terms, rather than as new asks.

# MEMORANDUM

**To:** Deal Team, Givand Battery Recovery, LLC matter
**From:** [Associate]
**Date:** November 11, 2026
**Re:** Buyer-side issues list: Goulound Lithium Reclamation asset purchase (APA dated September 22, 2026)

---

## Bottom Line

The APA's indemnity package looks buyer-friendly on paper. It has a 10% cap, with carve-outs for Fraud, Fundamental Representations and Excluded Liabilities, including Pre-Closing Environmental Liabilities. The Escrow Agreement undercuts that package in two ways:

- It turns the $4,850,000 escrow into Givand's only source of recovery.
- It moves escrow disputes to New York law and Manhattan courts.

APA Section 11.10 gives the Escrow Agreement control on "matters concerning the Escrow Fund," so the APA does not override either problem.

Separately:

- The Pellancourt offtake consent, which drives the deal value, is not a Required Consent or a closing condition.
- Seller can assign its post-closing obligations to anyone and be released.

All four items should be in our first-turn comments. Items 1 through 3 should be discussed with the client before we respond.

---

## Issues List (most significant first)

### 1. Escrow is the "sole and exclusive source of recovery," which removes the APA cap carve-outs. Priority: HIGH. Raise with client.

**Where:** Indemnity Escrow Agreement, Section 4.6. It works together with APA Sections 9.5(b), 9.7 and 11.10.

**What it says:** Section 4.6 makes the Escrow Fund Buyer's "sole and exclusive source of recovery for all Losses of the Buyer Indemnitees under Article IX … including Losses arising from Excluded Liabilities." The only exception is Fraud.

**Why it matters:**

- **The carve-outs are effectively removed.** APA Section 9.5(b) lifts the 10% cap for Fundamental Representations and Excluded Liabilities, including Pre-Closing Environmental Liabilities. APA Section 9.7 says escrow is the first source of recovery "and thereafter directly by Seller." Section 4.6 contradicts that. APA Section 11.10 says the Escrow Agreement controls on "matters concerning the Escrow Fund," so Seller will argue that Section 4.6 governs.
- **Environmental exposure is the most serious consequence.** Hazardous waste storage and treatment, solvent extraction and wastewater pretreatment have operated at the Sparks facility since at least 2021. Legacy contamination could easily exceed $4.85M. The LOI (Section 6) expressly promised uncapped recovery for retained environmental liabilities.
- **Recovery could drop to zero after release.** The escrow releases 18 months after Closing (Escrow Agreement Section 3.1). Fundamental Representations survive to the statute of limitations plus 60 days, and environmental representations survive six years (APA Section 9.1). Read literally, Section 4.6 would leave Givand with no recovery for any claim made after the release date, even within the survival period.

**Recommended fix:**

- **First position:** delete Section 4.6.
- **Fallback:** replace it with the following:

> "4.6 *Recovery.* The Escrow Fund is the first, but not the exclusive, source of recovery for Losses of the Buyer Indemnitees under Article IX of the Purchase Agreement. Nothing in this Agreement limits, expands or modifies the rights or remedies of the Buyer Indemnitees under the Purchase Agreement, including Sections 9.5(b) and 9.7 thereof, or Seller's obligation to pay any Losses directly to the extent not satisfied from the Escrow Fund."

- **APA Section 11.10:** narrow the escrow carve-out to the Escrow Agent's ministerial duties only. Suggested wording: "except that the Escrow Agreement shall control solely with respect to the rights, duties and obligations of the Escrow Agent; nothing in the Escrow Agreement shall limit the indemnification rights of the Buyer Indemnitees under Article IX."

**Client point:** confirm that Givand has not informally agreed to an escrow-only recovery construct. Ask whether the client wants to seek a longer or separate environmental holdback, or R&W/environmental insurance, given the 18-month release.

---

### 2. The Pellancourt consent is not a Required Consent or a closing condition. Priority: HIGH. Raise with client.

**Where:** Disclosure Schedule, Schedule 6.2(c) (Required Consents). It works together with Schedule 3.9, Item 1, Schedule 3.3(b), and APA Sections 6.2(c), 6.4 and 7.2(d).

**What it says:**

- **Schedule 3.9, Item 1:** under Section 16.2 of the Pellancourt Supply Agreement, a "change of control of Seller" or a transfer of all or substantially all of the recycling business assets requires Pellancourt's prior written consent. Under Section 16.3, Pellancourt may terminate on 30 days' notice if the transfer happens without consent. The schedule also states: "No consent has been requested or obtained."
- **Schedule 6.2(c):** "The only Required Consents are" the Facility landlord consent and the NDEP permit transfers. Pellancourt is not on the list.

**Why it matters:**

- **The transaction triggers the consent right.** It is a transfer of substantially all of the recycling business assets (APA Recital B).
- **Seller has no obligation to obtain the consent.** Seller's efforts covenant (APA Section 6.4) covers only Required Consents. The closing condition (APA Section 7.2(d)) does the same. Seller can therefore stand by while Givand faces a choice: close without the consent, or refuse to close and risk a breach claim.
- **The contract is central to the deal.** It is worth approximately $21M a year on a take-or-pay basis for at least 70% of refined output, running through 2030. The LOI calls it "a key reason for the Transaction." The LOI also states that Givand's valuation assumes it continues. LOI Section 9(c) expressly made the Pellancourt consent a closing condition, and the APA dropped it.
- **Termination after closing is not clearly indemnifiable.** Seller disclosed the consent right on Schedule 3.9 and Schedule 3.3(b), which qualifies the Section 3.3 no-conflicts representation.

**Recommended fix:**

- Amend Schedule 6.2(c) to add the following as a Required Consent: "3. the written consent of Pellancourt Cathode Materials, Inc. under Section 16.2 of the Pellancourt Supply Agreement to the assignment of the Pellancourt Supply Agreement to Buyer and the consummation of the transactions contemplated by the Agreement, together with a waiver of its termination right under Section 16.3, in form and substance reasonably satisfactory to Buyer."
- Add an express closing condition as APA Section 7.2(f), so that it survives even if the schedule is later revised.
- Strengthen Section 6.4 for this consent. Seller should begin outreach within 5 Business Days. Buyer should be allowed to join discussions with Pellancourt. Seller should bear any consent consideration Pellancourt demands, overriding the current "no consideration" language.
- **Fallback if Seller resists:** a specific indemnity for Losses from any Pellancourt termination or adverse renegotiation within 24 months after Closing, outside the cap. Alternatively, a purchase price adjustment or a separate holdback tied to receipt of the consent.

**Client point:** confirm whether Givand would ever close without Pellancourt. Ask whether Givand has a relationship with Pellancourt it wants to use directly.

---

### 3. The Escrow Agreement selects New York law and Manhattan courts, which conflicts with the APA's Delaware law and Chancery forum. Priority: HIGH.

**Where:** Indemnity Escrow Agreement, Section 9 (Governing Law; Jurisdiction), specifically Sections 9.1 and 9.2. It conflicts with APA Sections 11.7 and 11.8 and is reinforced by APA Section 11.10.

**What it says:**

- **Section 9.1:** New York law governs.
- **Section 9.2:** exclusive jurisdiction lies in state and federal courts in the Borough of Manhattan "for any dispute concerning the Escrow Fund, including whether a Claim Notice is valid or payable."
- **The APA:** chooses Delaware law (Section 11.7) and exclusive Court of Chancery jurisdiction (Section 11.8).
- **APA Section 11.10:** lets the Escrow Agreement control on escrow matters.

**Why it matters:**

- **Proceedings would split.** Every disputed Article IX claim asserted against the escrow could be litigated in New York under New York law. Any recovery above the escrow, such as carve-out claims and environmental claims, would be litigated in Delaware Chancery.
- **The risks:**
  - duplicative proceedings and costs;
  - inconsistent rulings on the same underlying breach;
  - a threshold fight over forum;
  - Seller arguing that a New York judgment on payability has preclusive effect in Delaware.
- **Defined terms would be read under different law.** "Fraud" is defined by reference to Delaware common law, but it would be construed by a New York court.
- **Final Orders are tied to the New York forum.** Escrow disbursements on a "Final Order" (Section 1.1) are tied to "a court … under Section 9," so a Delaware judgment may not qualify to release funds.

**Recommended fix:**

- Conform Escrow Agreement Section 9 to the APA:

> "9.1 This Agreement and all claims arising out of or relating to it are governed by the laws of the State of Delaware, without regard to conflict-of-laws principles … 9.2 Each Party irrevocably submits to the exclusive jurisdiction of the Court of Chancery of the State of Delaware (or, only if that court lacks subject-matter jurisdiction, the state or federal courts located in the State of Delaware) for any action arising out of or relating to this Agreement or the Escrow Fund, including whether a Claim Notice is valid or payable."

- Conform the "Final Order" definition to that forum.
- **If Ostrander insists on New York for its own protection:** limit New York law and forum to claims by or against the Escrow Agent in its capacity as such. All disputes between Buyer and Seller over Claim Notices should go to Delaware Chancery.
- Make the corresponding Section 11.10 change described in Item 1.

---

### 4. Seller can assign freely and is released on assignment; Buyer cannot assign without consent. Priority: MEDIUM-HIGH.

**Where:** APA, Section 11.4 (Assignment).

**What it says:**

- **Buyer's assignments:** Buyer needs Seller's consent for any assignment.
- **Seller's assignments:** Seller may assign the Agreement "including its obligations under Article IX, Section 6.7 and Section 6.8 and the Transition Services Agreement, to any Person without the consent of Buyer." Seller is "released from those obligations" once the assignee assumes them in writing.

**Why it matters:**

- **Givand could lose a creditworthy indemnitor.** After Closing, Seller will hold roughly $43.65M in cash proceeds. It could assign its indemnity obligations to a shell, distribute the cash, and leave Givand with only the escrow. Combined with Item 1, that makes the $4.85M the practical ceiling, and after the 18-month release the recovery is nothing.
- **The non-compete and TSA could move to a weak or adverse party.** These obligations could go to a thinly capitalized entity or to a direct competitor of Givand. The nine-month TSA covers accounting, IT, logistics and regulatory reporting, which is critical for the permit transition, and it could end up with an unwilling provider.
- **The clause is one-sided.** Givand cannot even assign to an affiliate or financing source, or to a later buyer of the business.

**Recommended fix:**

- Replace Section 11.4 with a mutual clause:

> "Neither Party may assign this Agreement or any of its rights or obligations under it without the prior written consent of the other Party, except that Buyer may, without Seller's consent, (a) assign any or all of its rights to one or more of its Affiliates, (b) collaterally assign its rights to any lender or financing source, and (c) assign its rights, in whole or in part, to any subsequent purchaser of all or any substantial part of the Business or the Purchased Assets. No assignment shall relieve the assigning Party of any of its obligations under this Agreement. Any purported assignment in violation of this Section 11.4 is void."

- **Fallback:** if Seller needs flexibility for its own wind-down or sale, consider the following conditions:
  - permit assignment by Seller only to a successor acquiring substantially all of Seller's assets, with Buyer's consent not unreasonably withheld;
  - no release of Seller;
  - the assignee must not be a competitor of Givand;
  - the assignee must expressly assume the obligations, including Section 6.7.
- Consider adding a Seller covenant to maintain minimum net worth, or not to dissolve or distribute proceeds below a set amount, during the general survival period. A parent or shareholder guaranty of Article IX obligations is an alternative.

**Client point:** ask whether Givand knows of Seller's post-closing plans, such as dissolution, distribution to shareholders or a sale of other businesses. That information will tell us how hard to push on the guaranty or net-worth covenant.

---

### 5. Related clean-up items. Priority: MEDIUM. Fold into the markup.
